lesson_title: Scissors That Only Cut One Thing: How Enzymes Digest Your Food
hook_text: Chew a piece of bread for a full minute. It starts to taste sweet. That is chemistry in your mouth.
clip_script: Chew bread for a minute and it turns sweet. Why? Your spit carries an enzyme, amylase, a tiny pair of molecular scissors that cuts starch into sugar. Enzymes are proteins, they are never used up, and each one cuts only one thing, like a key that fits one lock. Amylase cuts starch. Proteases cut protein. Lipases cut fat. They work best at 37 degrees, body temperature. Cold slows them down. Too much heat ruins their shape for good, like cooking an egg white, and they never work again. Now follow your food. Mouth: teeth chop, amylase starts on starch. Stomach: strong acid, pH 2, stops the amylase and lets pepsin start on protein. Small intestine: bile breaks fat into droplets, the pancreas pours in all three kinds of scissors, and the gut wall finishes the job. Starch becomes glucose. Protein becomes amino acids. Fat becomes fatty acids and glycerol. Three big, three small, straight into your blood.
visual_style: Close-up of bread being chewed with a sugar meter rising; cartoon scissors shaped like keys snip chains of beads; a thermometer swings from cold to 37 to 80 with the scissors slowing, working, then melting; the food travels mouth, stomach, intestine.
pacing: A tasting hook, a quick lock-and-key beat, a thermometer swing, a fast three-stop journey and a rhythmic finish.
